blocks.text: A report can filter tasks in several ways: by minimum priority, by completion state, or by a policy loaded from configuration. Runtime polymorphism lets the application use a stable interface while choosing an implementation during execution. It is valuable when the set of active behaviors is not fully fixed at the call site, but it also creates lifetime and substitution obligations.

blocks.text: Copying a derived object into a base object by value slices away the derived portion. blocks.text: Typical implementations use indirect dispatch machinery, often described in terms of virtual tables. The observable language contract is which override is selected and how lifetime behaves. Optimize the actual hot path later if indirect calls matter to the workload.

blocks.text: Virtual calls made during construction and destruction do not behave as calls on a fully initialized most-derived object at every stage. A base constructor should not rely on a derived override that needs derived members not yet initialized. Prefer explicit post-construction operations or composition when initialization would otherwise depend on such a call. This avoids making object validity depend on incomplete state.

blocks.text: Design the smallest useful interface. If a client only asks whether a sample is accepted, it should not also require every filter to expose a filename, network connection, mutable vector, and reset protocol. Broad interfaces make test implementations harder and force unrelated behaviors into every derived class. A narrow interface gives each implementation room to manage its own representation.

blocks.text: Document exceptional behavior as part of the interface. Can a query throw? Does it allocate? Can it retain input? Is it safe to call repeatedly? The compiler does not infer these domain promises from the word virtual. A later implementation that introduces a network request inside an apparently cheap predicate can dramatically change a report pipeline even while satisfying the function signature.

blocks.text: Avoid object slicing: storing a derived object by value in a base-valued collection would keep only the base portion, and an abstract base cannot serve that purpose at all. blocks.text: An owning pointer to a base must destroy the complete dynamic object correctly. The base destructor can be defaulted when it has no custom cleanup; its virtual nature is the important interface property.

topics.title: Failure clinic — The almost-matching override
topics.summary: A derived class writes bool accepts(int) while the base declares bool accepts(int) const. Without override, the code can introduce a different member and leave the class abstract or preserve an unexpected base implementation in a different hierarchy. With override, the compiler points directly at the mismatch. The correction is to match the intended interface, not to remove override to silence the diagnostic.

blocks.text: Another defect stores derived values in a vector<Base>. In a concrete base hierarchy this can slice each value, losing derived behavior. A vector of owning base pointers preserves the dynamic objects but changes the copy and allocation model. A variant can be an alternative when the set of implementations is closed and known at compile time. Chapter 19 develops that tradeoff rather than presenting inheritance as the only way to represent alternatives.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Runtime polymorphism selects behavior through an interface; it does not define copying, ownership, or error policy automatically. override catches signature mistakes. Base-value copying can slice. Virtual destruction is required by the chosen owning-base-pointer use. A small interface with explicit behavior is easier to substitute and test than a large base class that exposes every implementation detail.
